title: A T. rex Left Behind Its Footprints — And Scientists Are Thrilled
summary:
Tyrannosaurus rex fossils are pretty common — museums around the world display dozens of skeletons. But T. rex footprints? Those are incredibly rare. Dinosaur footprints usually don't survive millions of years, even when made by a 17,500-pound apex predator. That's what makes this discovery so remarkable.

Paleontologists from the Denver Museum of Nature & Science and Liverpool John Moores University have found four footprints along a 23-foot path in the Hell Creek Formation in southwestern North Dakota. It's the first known trackway made by an adult T. rex. The prints are about three feet long each — as long as a yardstick — and they date back roughly 66.5 million years.

The team found the tracks last year on federal land near Marmath, North Dakota, close to the Montana border. They carefully cleared the area and used a high-resolution 3D scanner to image each footprint. That let them analyze the scene digitally and create physical reproductions.

The two left and right prints suggest the dinosaur was a sizable adult with a 13-foot stride. But it wasn't in a hurry. Based on its gait, it was probably moseying along at 3.5 to 4.5 miles per hour — about the speed of a human power-walking. The scientists note that speed estimate is speculative, given the tracks' weathering.

"Bones tell us an enormous amount about these animals, but footprints capture a moment of behavior," said Tyler Lyson, a paleontologist at the Denver Museum and study co-author. "With a trackway, we can actually follow an animal as it moved across the landscape. That is incredibly rare for T. rex."

Later this year, the team plans to excavate three of the footprints and airlift them by helicopter to the Denver Museum of Nature & Science. Soon, you might be able to see these ancient steps in person — a literal trail left by one of the most fearsome dinosaurs to ever walk the Earth.
why_it_matters: This discovery shows how scientists can reconstruct behavior that bones cannot reveal — reading an animal's stride and walking speed from ancient footprints — and why preserving fossil-rich places matters for future discoveries.

background_read: Paleontologists at the Denver Museum of Nature & Science (a large natural-history museum in Colorado) and Liverpool John Moores University (a UK university with active dinosaur researchers) worked together on the find.
T. rex bones are widespread in museum collections, but footprints are easily destroyed by erosion, so an adult T. rex trackway offers a rare view of behavior rather than just anatomy.
The Hell Creek Formation (a fossil-rich rock layer in the American West from the last age of the dinosaurs) has produced many famous T. rex skeletons.
Footprints become fossils only if soft mud is buried and preserved before it erodes, which is why paleontologists value preserved steps as direct evidence of movement.
Scanning the prints before excavation let the team keep a digital record and share the site with scientists and the public without moving the original ground immediately.

perspectives.description: The trackway gives paleontologists direct behavioral data, such as stride and walking speed, that bones cannot provide. It is a rare window into how a huge dinosaur actually moved through its environment.
The number of tracks is small and the site is weathered, so any speed estimate is speculative. One individual's path may not represent all adult T. rex behavior.

Paleontology has this pattern of asymmetry: bones preserve common clues, while footprints preserve rare moments. Each find must be interpreted carefully and compared with better-preserved sites before firm conclusions are drawn.

The planned helicopter lift will make the footprints available to museum visitors and future researchers. The digital scans could also allow scientists anywhere to study the trackway and compare it with other dinosaur footprints.
